You are a literature-research subagent. Do NOT write any files. Return findings as your final text reply only. Use WebSearch and WebFetch (load them via ToolSearch "select:WebSearch,WebFetch" first). Work autonomously; no human will answer questions. Use American spelling.

TASK: Collect QUANTITATIVE empirical solar-wind trends usable as benchmarks for a 3D MHD heliospheric model spanning 0.1-2.5 AU. For each number give: paper (authors, year, journal), table/figure/section, and URL or DOI. Clearly flag anything you could not verify from the source text (no numbers from memory without saying so). Prefer open-access full texts (arXiv, AGU OA, A&A, ApJ OA, Living Reviews, Frontiers).

Topics:
1. Radial scalings from Helios/Ulysses/Voyager/PSP/Solar Orbiter: density n ∝ r^-2 (fitted exponents, e.g., Hellinger et al. 2011, 2013 Helios; Maksimovic et al. 2020 PSP; Perrone et al.), proton temperature T_p ∝ r^-α (α for slow and fast wind: Hellinger et al. 2011 JGR, 2013; Cranmer et al. 2009; Totten 1995; Gazis/Richardson for Voyager; Lopez & Freeman 1986 T-V relation T ∝ V^2), |B| and its radial components (B_r ∝ r^-2, B_t ∝ r^-1), the Parker spiral angle at 1 AU (~45 deg) and observed distributions, typical 1 AU values of n, v, T, |B| for slow and fast wind (e.g., Ebert et al. 2009 Ulysses; Schwenn 1990; McGregor et al. 2011), speed acceleration beyond 0.3 AU (e.g., Schwenn 1990 Helios slow wind accelerates ~?; Dakeyo et al. 2022 ApJ PSP+Helios+SolO speed profiles; Maksimovic 2020; Halekas et al. 2022/2023 PSP), and the 1/r^2 scaling of mass flux. Also proton-flux invariance with distance.
2. n-v anticorrelation at 1 AU and the near-constancy of the energy flux or momentum flux with speed: Le Chat, Issautier & Meyer-Vernet 2012 Solar Physics "The solar wind energy flux" (value of W ~ 1.5e-3 W/m^2 normalized? or 70 W/m^2 at Rsun?), Wang 2010 ApJL (momentum flux / mass flux vs speed), McGregor et al. 2011 JGR (relations used to set ENLIL boundary density, n v^2 = const or n v = const?), Schwadron & McComas, Meyer-Vernet 2007. Also the momentum-flux relation used in WSA-ENLIL / EUHFORIA boundary (n v^2 = const; T ∝ v ... in ENLIL n v^2 const, n T const).
3. CIR/SIR statistics vs heliocentric distance: Jian, Russell, Luhmann, Skoug 2006 Solar Physics (1 AU SIR statistics: occurrence rate per year/rotation, fraction with shocks (~?%), typical peak Pt, peak N, peak B, speed increase), Jian et al. 2008 (STEREO/Venus Express at 0.72 AU; SIR statistics vs distance), Jian et al. 2019 Solar Physics (STEREO 2007-2016, SIR shock fraction), Jian et al. 2008 Ulysses/Venus, Richardson 2018 Living Reviews in Solar Physics "Solar wind stream interaction regions throughout the heliosphere" (shock occurrence vs distance: e.g., few % at 0.3 AU, ~25% at 1 AU, ~90% by 4-5 AU; Helios/Ulysses/Pioneer results), Allen et al. 2021 A&A (PSP SIR statistics), Allen et al. 2020/2021 SIR at PSP; Gosling & Pizzo 1999 Space Sci Rev 89, 21 (CIR shock formation beyond 2-3 AU); Hundhausen 1973; Smith & Wolfe 1976 (Pioneer 10/11: compression grows with distance, shock pairs beyond ~2-3 AU); Mason et al. Also how peak density/pressure enhancement and SIR shock fraction grow from 1 to 2 AU (Mars at 1.5 AU: e.g., Huang et al., Geyer et al. 2021 MAVEN SIR statistics; Jian?).

Return a compact but complete markdown report (up to ~1800 words) organized by topic, with a summary table of target values (quantity, value, distance range, source, URL). Flag unverified numbers explicitly.

Only a SubagentHandback call reaches your caller as your result; plain text you write at the end is not delivered. Do not also send the report with SendMessage: your caller would get it twice.

Links: [{"title":"flore.unifi.it","url":"https://flore.unifi.it/handle/2158/600050"},{"title":"cas.cz","url":"https://www.asu.cas.cz/~helinger/hellal11.pdf"},{"title":"cas.cz","url":"https://www.asu.cas.cz/~helinger/hellal13.pdf"},{"title":"Hellinger JGR v116 2011","url":"https://helios-data.ssl.berkeley.edu/data/Miscellaneous_Documentation/Some_Science_Papers_using_Helios_data/Hellinger_JGR_v116_2011.pdf"},{"title":"item 1898896 1","url":"https://pure.mpg.de/pubman/item/item_1898896_1"},{"title":"EarthRef.org Reference Database (ERR)","url":"https://earthref.org/ERR/155930"},{"title":"Hellinger JGRA v118 2013","url":"https://helios-data.ssl.berkeley.edu/data/Miscellaneous_Documentation/Some_Science_Papers_using_Helios_data/Hellinger_JGRA_v118_2013.pdf"},{"title":"helios-data.ssl.berkeley.edu","url":"https://helios-data.ssl.berkeley.edu/data/Miscellaneous_Documentation/Some_Science_Papers_using_Helios_data/Title%20Query%20Results.pdf"},{"title":"SPRG Seminars","url":"https://cdaweb.gsfc.nasa.gov/data/fast/documents/archived_websites/sprg.ssl.berkeley.edu/seminars/seminars_2013-03-12.html"}]

The search turned up the paper's abstract and metadata but not its fitted radial exponents, so I can't confirm the specific power-law values.

- **Publication:** Hellinger, Matteini, Štverák, Trávníček, and Marsch, *Journal of Geophysical Research*, vol. 116, A09105, 2011 (doi:10.1029/2011JA016674). Received 21 March 2011; revised 24 May 2011; accepted 27 June 2011; published 27 September 2011.
- **Main finding:** Closer to the Sun, the parallel and perpendicular proton temperature profiles imply the need for parallel cooling and perpendicular heating. Around 1 AU, heating is needed in both directions. Closer to the Sun, it is estimated that, to account for the observed radial profiles of the proton parallel and perpendicular temperature, nonnegligible parallel cooling and perpendicular heating are necessary. Around 1 AU heating is needed in both directions.
- **Radial power law:** The paper's reference point is the adiabatic scaling of total proton temperature with heliocentric distance R. Observed temperatures fall off more slowly than that scaling, which the authors take as evidence for efficient proton heating. Helios observations show that the total proton temperature falls off more slowly than what is expected from the adiabatic prediction (i.e., T ∝ R−4/3). This suggests a need for efficient proton heating.
- **Double-adiabatic contrast:** Weakly collisional fast-wind protons would be expected to follow double-adiabatic (CGL) evolution, which gives a different radial dependence. Observed protons deviate from it. Solar wind protons do not follow the double adiabatic prediction; their perpendicular temperature decreases with distance more slowly, whereas the parallel temperature decreases faster.
- **Energy budget:** The authors conclude that significant interplanetary heating is needed overall, and they also evaluate how deceleration of fast streams interacting with slow ones could affect proton thermodynamics.
- **Follow-up:** A 2013 paper, "Proton thermal energetics in the solar wind: Helios reloaded," extends the analysis to the slow wind. In the parallel direction, protons need to be cooled at 0.3 AU, with a cooling rate comparable to the corresponding perpendicular heating rate.

For the exact fitted exponents, see the full text at the Czech group's copy (asu.cas.cz/~helinger/hellal11.pdf) or the Berkeley Helios archive copy.

The review is Ian G. Richardson's "Solar wind stream interaction regions throughout the heliosphere," in *Living Reviews in Solar Physics* (2018, vol. 15, art. 1). It was published online on January 26, 2018, with DOI 10.1007/s41116-017-0011-z, and it is open access.

- **Scope:** It covers stream interaction regions (SIRs) formed where fast wind from coronal holes overtakes slower wind ahead of it. These regions corotate with the Sun and can persist for many solar rotations.
- **Observations reviewed:** Helios data from about 0.3 to 1 AU, Pioneer 10 and 11 and Voyager 1 and 2 in the outer heliosphere, and Ulysses data out of the ecliptic.
- **Physical effects:** SIRs accelerate energetic particles, modulate galactic cosmic ray intensity, and produce enhanced geomagnetic activity.
- **Methods:** The review also discusses remote detection with interplanetary scintillation and white-light imaging, plus MHD modeling of SIRs.

The search returned only the abstract and metadata, not the full text, so I couldn't check the body sections. Later papers in the results, such as the 2018 ApJL on merging SIRs by Wang et al. and the 2021 PSP SIR catalog, cite this review as the standard reference.

The paper you're looking for is Dakeyo, Maksimovic, Démoulin, Halekas, and Stevens (2022), published in The Astrophysical Journal as volume 940, article 130, DOI 10.3847/1538-4357/ac9b14. Its arXiv preprint is 2207.03898, submitted July 8, 2022.

- **Data and finding:** The authors classified Helios solar wind observations by bulk speed and extended that classification closer to the Sun using Parker Solar Probe data. The known speed-temperature correlations hold in the PSP data, and the slowest winds still accelerate. The paper shows that recent PSP measurements are compatible with an extension closer to the Sun of the Helios classification. The bulk speed/proton temperature correlation and the bulk speed/electron temperature anticorrelation, along with the acceleration of the slowest winds, are verified in PSP data.
- **Model:** The authors fit an "iso-poly" model, which is isothermal in the corona and then polytropic beyond the sonic point. The polytropic indices are derived from the observed temperature and density gradients.
- **Follow-up work:** A 2025 bipoly paper (arXiv 2503.01782) builds on the isopoly approach and cites the 2022 paper along with a 2024 Dakeyo et al. paper. A 2026 PSP study (arXiv 2609.00318) also overlays iso-poly curves citing Dakeyo et al. 2022.

I did not check the 2024 Dakeyo paper or the full text of the 2022 article for specific numerical results.

HELLINGER ET AL: PROTON THERMAL ENERGETICS
3.1.
Solar wind variations
Here we use data from ion analyzers and ﬂuxgate magnetome-
ters onboard the Helios 1 and 2 spacecraft [Marsch et al., 1982a, b,
and references therein]. The Helios analyzers employ a quadri-
spherical ion electrostatic deﬂector that analyses ions with respect
to their charge-per-energy ratio. A full three-dimensional spectrum,
32 channels (exponentially distributed between 155 V and 15.3 kV)
times 9 × 16 angular channels (with the resolution 5o × 5o making
use of the spacecraft rotation) is measured every 40.5 s. In this pa-
per we use these 3-D energy spectra to calculate the basic moments
of the proton velocity distribution function; the contribution of al-
pha particles is removed by using their different charge-to-mass ra-
tio [Marsch et al., 1982b]. We calculate the proton number density,
n, radial component of the mean velocity, vR, parallel and perpen-
dicular temperatures, T∥and T⊥, and both non-zero components
of the heat ﬂux tensor, q∥and q⊥. Note that the temperatures and
heat ﬂuxes are calculated for the whole observed proton distribu-
tion functions. A possible secondary proton population contributes
to the parallel temperature and to the heat ﬂuxes.
We start our data analysis with some typical radial proﬁles of
observed solar wind quantities. Figure 1 displays the radial pro-
ﬁles of the proton radial velocity vR, the magnitude of the mag-
netic ﬁeld B, and the proton density n, as observed by Helios 1
from January to March in 1976. Only selected data are used, for
which it is easily possible to separate the proton and alpha-particle
contributions in the 3-D velocity spectra. Figure 1 illustrates some
general features of the solar wind in the ecliptic plane: the solar
wind is characterized by alternating slow and fast streams. The
magnitude of the magnetic ﬁeld decreases with the radial distance
R. The proton density and the radial velocity exhibit a well known
anti-correlation.
Figure 1. Helios 1: Points show (top) proton radial velocity
vR, (middle) magnitude of the magnetic ﬁeld B, (bottom) pro-
ton density n as a function of the radial distance R during a part
of the spacecraft trajectory (from January to March in 1976).
Figure 2, laid out in the same format as Figure 1, shows the ra-
dial proﬁles of the parallel and perpendicular proton temperatures,
T∥and T⊥, as well as of the averaged proton temperature T ob-
served by Helios 1 from January to March in 1976. Figure 2 illus-
trates the well known correlation between the proton temperature
and the velocity [cf., Elliott et al., 2010], which holds also for the
parallel and perpendicular proton temperatures.
Figure 2. Helios 1: Points show (top) parallel proton temper-
ature T∥, (middle) perpendicular proton temperature T⊥, and
(bottom) average proton temperature T as a function of the ra-
dial distance R during a part of the spacecraft trajectory (from
January to March in 1976, same as in Figure 1).
3.2.
Radial dependencies
Following Cranmer et al. [2009] we try to determine the radial
dependence of the parallel and perpendicular temperatures in the
fast solar wind, in order to estimate the energy balance of the pro-
tons. We use the whole data set of 3-D ion energy spectra from both
Helios spacecrafts, but select only those data where it was easy to
separate alpha-particles from protons. Here we only investigate the
fast solar wind. Therefore, we have selected only those cases in
which the proton radial velocity vR > 600 km/s.
Figure 3. Helios 1 & 2 observations: Points show (top) proton
radial velocity vR, (middle) magnitude of the magnetic ﬁeld B,
(bottom) proton density n as a function of the radial distance R.
Overplotted solid curves show the ﬁtted results (see the text).

Abstract.
The proton thermal energetics in the slow solar wind between 0.3 and 1 AU is
re-investigated using the Helios 1 and 2 data, complementing a similar analysis for the fast
solar wind [Hellinger et al., 2011]. The results for slow and fast solar winds are compared
and discussed in the context of previous results. Protons need to be heated in the perpendic-
ular direction with respect the ambient magnetic ﬁeld from 0.3 to 1 AU. In the parallel di-
rection protons need to be cooled at 0.3 AU with a cooling rate comparable to the correspond-
ing perpendicular heating rate; between 0.3 and 1 AU the required cooling rate decreases un-
til a transition to heating occurs: by 1 AU the protons require parallel heating, with a heat-
ing rate comparable to that required to sustain the perpendicular temperature. The heating/cooling
rates (per unit volume) in the fast and slow solar winds are proportional to the ratio between
the proton kinetic energy and the expansion time. On average the protons need to be heated
and the necessary heating rates are comparable to the energy cascade rate of the magnetohy-
drodynamic turbulence estimated from the stationary Kolmogorov-Yaglom law at 1 AU; how-
ever, in the expanding solar wind the stationarity assumption for this law is questionable. The
turbulent energy cascade may explain the average proton energetics (although the stationar-
ity assumption needs to be justiﬁed) but the parallel cooling is likely related to microinsta-
bilities connected with the structure of the proton velocity distribution function. This is sup-
ported by linear analysis based on observed data and by results of numerical simulations.
